text: Just below a boil: small, lazy bubbles breaking the surface now and then. Gentle enough to keep meat tender and sauces from catching.
Turn a light mixture into a heavier one with slow scoops of a spatula, cutting down through the middle and lifting over, so the air you whipped in stays put.
Cook quickly in a little hot fat, keeping things moving so they colour without stewing.
The thin coloured skin of a citrus fruit, finely grated or pared, where all the fragrant oil lives. Stop before the bitter white pith.
Leave food sitting in a seasoned, often acidic, liquid (the marinade) so it soaks up flavour. Longer isn't always better: fish wants minutes, beef can take a night.
Scrape out the seeds, and with chillies the pale ribs too, which is where most of the heat hides.
Squeeze a soft mixture (cream, icing, choux, mash) through a bag and nozzle to shape it neatly.
In a British recipe, the oven's fierce top heat that browns from above. In an American one, cooking over the bars of a barbecue.
American for cooking under the oven's top element, close and hot, to brown or blister the top fast. Keep an eye on it: seconds separate golden from charcoal.
Cook slowly until the natural sugars brown and turn deep, sweet and nutty. Onions take a good half hour; there's no rushing them.
Push, fold and turn a dough over and over until it goes smooth and springy, which builds the gluten that holds bread up.
Shake dry ingredients through a sieve to break up lumps and mix them evenly, with a little air for good measure.
Beat hard and fast to force air in, until cream or egg whites thicken and hold their shape.
A shiny coat brushed or spooned on: egg on pastry, sticky sauce on meat, sugar syrup on cake.
Work cold fat into flour with a pastry cutter or two knives until it looks like coarse crumbs, leaving tiny pieces of butter for flaky pastry.
Blacken in patches over high heat for a smoky, slightly bitter edge. Patches, mind, not the whole thing.
Toss small, evenly cut pieces in a very hot wok with a splash of oil, a minute or two at a time, so they sear rather than stew.
Cook fully submerged in hot oil, usually 170 to 190°C. Use a deep pan no more than a third full, and a thermometer if you have one.
Leave a yeasted dough somewhere warm to rise. It's ready when it has roughly doubled and a floured finger leaves a dent that springs back slowly.
Brown the outside hard in a very hot pan for colour and flavour. Leave it alone until it releases by itself.
Whipped cream or egg white that holds a peak when you lift the whisk, but the tip flops over.
Whipped until the peaks stand straight up and the bowl could (bravely) be held upside down.
Spoon the pan's hot fat or juices over food as it cooks, to keep it moist and help it brown.
With the stone taken out: cherries, olives, plums, dates.
With the stone (the pit) taken out.
Let something sit in a hot or cold liquid until its flavour moves across, like tea, but with vanilla, herbs or spices.
Italian for 'to the tooth': pasta or rice cooked through with a slight bite left in the middle.
Make shallow cuts across the surface, so fat crisps, marinade gets in, or bread opens where you want it to.
Lift the foam or fat off the surface of a simmering liquid with a spoon or ladle.
A boneless piece of fish or meat, or the job of cutting it off the bone.
The vegetables, herbs and spices cooked first to build flavour: onion, garlic, ginger, celery and the like.
Salty water, sometimes sweetened and spiced, that meat soaks in before cooking so it stays juicy.
Plunge into boiling water briefly, then usually straight into cold. It sets colour, loosens skins and part-cooks.
Pinch or press the edge of pastry into a pattern, which seals it and looks the part.
Cut into thin, even matchsticks, about the size of a long matchstick or thinner.
Cook gently in liquid that's barely trembling, well below a boil, for delicate things like eggs, fish and fruit.
Chunky sticks, thicker than matchsticks, roughly the size of a chip.
Take the green top and stalky core out of a strawberry.
Beat butter and sugar together until pale and fluffy, which traps the air that lifts a cake. It takes longer than you think.
Coax fat and water, which don't want to mix, into one smooth, creamy sauce, usually by adding one slowly to the other while whisking.
Rub cold butter into flour with your fingertips until it looks like breadcrumbs. Keep it quick and light so the butter doesn't melt.
Equal parts fat and flour cooked together, the base that thickens white sauce, gravy and gumbo. The longer it cooks, the darker and nuttier it gets.
Pull out the dark gut thread running down a prawn's back.
Pour liquid into a hot pan and scrape up the browned bits stuck to the bottom. That's where the flavour is.
Coat lightly in flour or crumbs, shaking off the extra, before frying.
Brown, then cook low and slow, covered, in a little liquid, until tough cuts give up and go tender.
Cook over high heat until the skin puffs and splits in dark spots: tomatoes, peppers, green beans.
Cook gently in a little fat, often with a lid on, until soft and translucent without any colour.
Wake an ingredient up before using it: gelatine soaked in cold water, spices fried briefly in hot oil, yeast frothed in warm water.
Peel or cut away a thin layer, such as a strip of citrus peel without the pith.
Cook fatty meat slowly so the fat melts out and the rest crisps up.
Leave fruit sitting in sugar, juice or alcohol until it softens and gives up its juices.
Beaten egg, sometimes with a splash of milk or water, brushed on pastry or bread for a golden shine.
Eggs and sugar whisked until thick and pale enough that a trail dropped from the whisk sits on top for a few seconds.
Cut citrus into clean wedges with no skin, pith or membrane: peel with a knife, then slice either side of each divider.
Cornflour (or another starch) mixed smooth with a little cold liquid, stirred into a hot sauce to thicken it without lumps.
Pour a shaken drink through the shaker's strainer and a fine tea strainer at once, to catch ice chips and bits of fruit or herb.
Slice almost all the way through and open out flat like a book, so it cooks evenly and fast.
Preserve and season with salt (often sugar too, sometimes smoke), drawing moisture out: think bacon, gravlax, prosciutto.
Scatter small pieces, usually of butter, over the top.
Press the air out of a risen dough before shaping it.
Diced onion, carrot and celery, cooked slowly as the flavour base for stocks, soups and stews.
Three meanings: heat and cool chocolate so it sets glossy and snaps; warm eggs with a little hot liquid so they don't scramble; fry whole spices in hot fat to pour over a dish.
Bake a pastry case empty, weighed down with baking beans on paper, so the base cooks crisp before the filling goes in.
Press fruit, herbs or sugar in the bottom of a glass or shaker with a muddler or the end of a rolling pin, to release juice and oils. Press, don't pulverise: mint turns bitter.
Butter melted gently and the milky solids left behind, so it can take high heat without burning.
A bowl set over a pan of barely simmering water, not touching it, for melting chocolate or cooking delicate sauces gently.
A tin of hot water that a dish sits in while it bakes, or a bowl over simmering water, so the heat stays gentle and custards don't split.
Cut the backbone out of a bird and press it flat, so it cooks evenly and much faster.
Cook slowly submerged in fat at a low heat, classically duck legs, until meltingly tender.
Boil briefly until part cooked, before finishing another way. The secret of crisp roast potatoes.
Pour in spirit and set it alight to burn off the alcohol. Turn the extractor fan off and keep your eyebrows well back.
Butter cooked past melted until the solids turn golden and it smells of toasted hazelnuts. Seconds from burnt, so watch it.
Sprinkle a fine, light layer, usually of flour, icing sugar or cocoa, through a sieve.
Chopped as finely as you can, almost to a paste (garlic, ginger, herbs). With meat, put through a grinder.
American for a sweet, spreadable cake covering, usually butter or cream cheese beaten with sugar.
Non-stick paper for lining tins and trays.
Non-stick paper for lining tins and trays so nothing welds itself on.
A frying pan, often cast iron, with sloped or straight sides.
A wide, shallow pan with sloping sides for frying.
Everyday wheat flour with no raising agent added.
Everyday wheat flour with no raising agent added.
Flour with baking powder already mixed in. No self-raising? Add 2 teaspoons of baking powder to 150 g plain flour.
The fresh green herb, bright and citrusy (or soapy, if your genes say so).
The dried seeds of the coriander plant, whole or ground: warm and orangey, nothing like the leaves.
The fresh leaves of the coriander plant.
Fine white sugar that dissolves fast, which is why bakers love it.
Caster sugar that's less refined, with a faint caramel flavour and colour. Plain caster sugar works fine instead.
Fine white sugar that dissolves fast.
Sugar ground to a soft powder, for icings and dusting.
Sugar ground to a soft powder, with a little cornflour to stop it clumping.
A savoury liquid made by simmering meat, bones or vegetables.
A flat metal tray for the oven, often with a low rim.
A flat metal tray for the oven; a sheet pan has a rim, a cookie sheet often doesn't.
Coarse, flaky salt that's easy to pinch. It's less salty by the spoonful than fine salt, so use a bit less fine salt in its place.
Rich cream, around 48% fat, that whips well and won't split when boiled.
Rich cream, about 36% fat or more, that whips well.
Thin pouring cream, about 18% fat. It won't whip and may split if boiled.
American mix of milk and cream, about 12% fat. Half milk, half single cream does the job.
Cream thickened and soured with a culture: tangy and spoonable.
Thick, slightly soured French cream that, unlike soured cream, can be boiled without splitting (the full-fat one, at least).
Very thick, rich cream from Devon and Cornwall, heated slowly until a golden crust forms. Made for scones.
A pitcher, or a measuring cup with a spout.
Young onions with a small white bulb and long green tops, both eaten.
Young onions with a small white bulb and long green tops, both eaten.
Fine white starch from maize, for thickening sauces and making things crisp. Not the yellow cornmeal.
Fine white starch from maize, for thickening and crisping.
Absorbent paper towel on a roll, for draining and patting dry.
A heavy, lidded pot, usually cast iron, that goes on the hob and in the oven.
A spoonful piled up as high as it'll go, rather than levelled off.
A touch less than the amount given.
In a British recipe, concentrated tomato paste from a tube or tin. Careful: American 'tomato puree' is thinner, more like passata.
Thick, concentrated tomato. A spoonful fried for a minute adds deep savoury flavour.
Smooth, sieved raw tomatoes, sold in jars and cartons: no seeds, no skins, no lumps.
Dried crushed chillies, seeds and all.
Dried crushed chillies, seeds and all. Not sweet peppers.
Moist, fine brown sugar with a gentle caramel taste.
Moist brown sugar with more molasses in it: darker, stickier and more toffee-like.
Meat put through a grinder.
Meat put through a grinder.
A deep, sturdy tray for roasting meat and vegetables.
Mild, all-purpose cooking oil. Cold-pressed it's golden and grassy.
Mild, neutral cooking oil.
A raising agent that needs something acidic in the mix (buttermilk, yoghurt, lemon) to fizz. Not the same as baking powder.
A raising agent that needs an acid in the mix to work. Not baking powder.
A metal tin for baking cakes in.
A deep rectangular tin for loaves and loaf cakes; a '2 lb' tin holds about 900 g of dough.
A round tin whose side unclips from the base, so cheesecakes and tortes come out in one piece.
A shallow round cake tin, usually used in pairs for a layered sponge like a Victoria sandwich.
A small, round, straight-sided ovenproof dish for one: soufflés, crème brûlée, little pots of anything.
A cone of plastic or cloth with a nozzle at the tip, for piping. A food bag with a corner snipped off works in a pinch.
A long, flat, blunt blade, often bent near the handle, for spreading icing and lifting delicate things.
A wide, slotted turner for flipping and lifting.
A heavy bowl and club for crushing spices, garlic and herbs. Slower than a blender and much better for it.
A slicer with an adjustable blade for paper-thin, even slices. Use the guard; it bites.
A very sharp, fine grater for zest, hard cheese, nutmeg and garlic.
A heavy, ridged pan that gives food charred stripes. In America a griddle is a flat plate.
Thin, stretchy plastic for wrapping and covering.
British gas oven settings: mark 4 is about 180°C or 350°F, and each mark up adds roughly 14°C.
An oven with a fan that moves the heat around, so it cooks hotter: set it about 20°C lower than a conventional oven.
The cooking rings or plates on top of the cooker.
The burners on top of the stove.
A young green summer squash.
A young green summer squash.
The glossy purple vegetable that soaks up oil like a sponge.
The glossy purple vegetable.
Peppery salad leaves.
Peppery salad leaves.
The deep red root, sold raw or cooked. It stains everything it touches.
A big, yellow-fleshed root with a purple top, sweet and earthy once cooked.
Flat pea pods eaten whole, peas and all.
Big, pale green beans. Slip off the grey skins after cooking for the bright ones inside.
A Chinese cabbage with white stalks and dark leaves, juicy and mild.
Nutty round pulses, the base of hummus. Keep the can's liquid: that's aquafaba.
What British recipes call shrimp of any size.
What American recipes call prawns of any size.
Bacon cut from the belly, with stripes of fat. It's what Americans just call bacon.
Leaner British bacon from the loin with a tail of belly, the usual for a fry-up.
A slice of bacon.
Little batons of bacon or pancetta, fried until crisp.
Cured raw ham, from the back leg of the pig, that you cook yourself.
Seasoned sausage filling without the casing.
A whole potato baked in its skin until crisp outside and fluffy in.
Thin fried potato slices from a packet.
Thick, amber, buttery-tasting sugar syrup from a tin. Light corn syrup is the nearest swap, with a little honey for flavour.
Dark, thick, bittersweet syrup left from refining sugar.
Dark, thick, bittersweet syrup left from refining sugar.
Large golden crystals with a light toffee taste, good for crunchy tops.
Unrefined, sticky brown sugar with a deep treacly flavour.
A British sweet blend, mostly cinnamon with nutmeg, allspice, cloves and ginger. Pumpkin pie spice is close.
Cherries preserved in syrup until sweet and chewy: the bright red ones in fruit cake.
Chopped candied citrus peel, for fruit cakes and buns.
Pale golden dried grapes, plumper and sweeter than raisins.
Finely grated, dried, unsweetened coconut.
Almonds sliced into thin petals.
Almonds ground to a fine meal: moist, rich and gluten-free in bakes. Almond flour is the finer, blanched version.
The dried seed pod of a vanilla orchid. Split it and scrape out the tiny black seeds; then infuse the pod too.
High-protein flour that builds more gluten, for chewy bread with a good rise.
Flour milled from the whole wheat grain, bran and all: nutty, heavier and thirstier.
Concentrated stock, as a cube, pot or powder, dissolved in hot water. Usually salty, so season after.
Oat grains steamed and flattened into flakes.
Crumbly, lightly sweet wholemeal biscuits, the classic cheesecake base. Graham crackers are the American cousin.
Sweet American wholewheat crackers, crushed for pie crusts. Digestive biscuits are the nearest British swap.
Small cucumbers pickled in vinegar.
Oil pressed from peanuts: mild, and happy at high heat.
Hard fat from around beef kidneys (or a vegetable version), for suet pastry and dumplings with that light, crumbly texture.
British for dark chocolate. Look for around 70% cocoa solids unless the recipe says otherwise.
An unmeasured lump of butter, about a tablespoon or so. Nobody's counting.
American butter sold in quarter-pound sticks: one stick is 113 g, or 8 tablespoons.
Ceramic beads (or dried beans or rice) that weigh down pastry while it bakes blind.
A shaped cutter for stamping out pastry or biscuits; in America, also a hand tool of wires for cutting butter into flour.
Sugar dissolved in water, usually one to one, for sweetening drinks evenly. Rich syrup is two to one.
Strong, bitter-aromatic extracts of herbs and spices, measured in dashes. They round a drink out the way salt does food.
The liquid from a tin of chickpeas. It whips like egg white, so it's the vegan foam in sours and meringues.
A stemmed glass with a broad, shallow bowl, for drinks served up without ice.
A tall, straight glass for long drinks over lots of ice; a Collins glass is a little taller and narrower.
A metal tin (or a tin and a glass) for shaking drinks with ice. A big jar with a tight lid will do.
